passage.text:
Night markets notice
The night markets team needs helpers on Saturday. Bring gloves and arrive before nine.

Message from a friend
I have booked the street food session for Tuesday, but I may arrive late. Please start without me and save a place.

Information sign
Visitors to the night markets may use the tools, but they must return them before leaving.

Short announcement
The visitors meeting has moved from Room 2 to Room 4 because the first room is being painted.

Notice for members
Members can borrow one street food guide for a week. Ask at the desk if you need another copy.

passage.text: The people below want to choose from night markets and street food. Decide which option is most suitable.

passage.label: A
passage.text: Evening street food tasting walk — A guided evening walk that stops at six popular stalls for a taste of local specialities. The group is kept under ten, booking opens one week ahead, and the route covers about two kilometres. Guests should bring small change because several stalls only accept cash.

passage.label: B
passage.text: Seated vegetarian tasting night — A relaxed evening meal in a covered food hall where diners sit at shared tables and receive eight small vegetarian dishes served over two hours. Every plate lists its main ingredients, and staff describe each dish. Tables stand close to the entrance, so guests hardly walk at all, and students pay a reduced price.

passage.label: C
passage.text: Family lantern food evening — An outdoor evening event in the park with lantern making, soft music and games for young children. A separate children's menu avoids spicy dishes, the fun ends at quarter to nine, and children under ten enter free. Parents stay together and each child receives a small lantern to keep.

passage.label: D
passage.text: Weekend market stall helper — A Sunday volunteer shift at a busy market stall that teaches useful skills and finishes with a free hot meal for every helper. Newcomers are welcome, training takes ten minutes, and the work includes carrying some heavy boxes. Helpers must be at least sixteen years old.

passage.label: E
passage.text: Midnight street food crawl — Four cheap snack stops after eleven at night, served from standing counters by the river. Each stop offers a different unusual flavour, a student card takes money off every plate, and the last counter closes at one. Cash and cards are accepted, a drink is included, and portions are generous, so arrive hungry.

passage.label: F
passage.text: Early morning food photography — A quiet weekday morning in the market before the crowds arrive, when the light is soft and stalls still stand half empty. A photographer shows you angles for every dish and answers questions; you need your own camera. The visit is unhurried and ends before nine.

passage.label: G
passage.text: Two hour cooking masterclass — An evening masterclass where a chef teaches you to prepare three dishes from scratch. All ingredients are supplied, the class is limited to eight people, and participants must be able to stand for the whole two hours. A course fee is charged, and an apron is provided.

passage.label: H
passage.text: Meat only food truck corner — An outdoor corner with three food trucks that serve only meat dishes, takeaway style, with no seating and no vegetarian choices. The trucks operate every evening but close at eight, and prices are moderate. Portions are large enough to share, and the menu changes each week.

questions.prompt: Nadia is vegetarian and cannot walk far because of a knee injury. She has one free evening this week, wants to taste many dishes without spending much, and prefers to sit rather than queue at stalls.
Tomas wants an outdoor evening with his two young children, who dislike spicy food and need to be home before nine. He hopes for something safe and lively near the park, with little walking.
Mei is a teenager with no cooking experience who wants weekend work where she can learn useful skills and receive a free meal. She is free on Sunday evenings and does not mind lifting heavy boxes.
Ravi is a student on a very small budget who finishes studying late and wants cheap midnight snacks. He is happy to eat standing up at a counter and enjoys trying unusual flavours.

Anja wants to photograph street food for her college portfolio and needs calm lighting before the crowds arrive. She is free on weekday mornings and would like a quiet, unhurried visit with expert tips on camera angles.

passage.text: When the visitors in our town started a night markets project, few residents expected it to grow so quickly. At first, the organisers met in a small room and planned one simple activity involving street food. They soon discovered that people were more willing to join when they could see a clear benefit for the neighbourhood. The organisers therefore published a short timetable and invited local businesses to offer practical help.

The project was not completely easy. Some volunteers were worried that the work would take too much time, while others wanted to change the plan every week. The team solved this by giving each person one small responsibility and reviewing the results together. This made the project feel manageable, and it also meant that new volunteers could contribute without special experience.

Looking back, the organiser says the most important lesson was not the final result but the way people learned to cooperate. The group still has problems, especially when the weather affects outdoor work, yet members now discuss solutions rather than blaming one another. For this reason, the project has become a useful example of how a modest local idea can create lasting connections.

parts.passageTitle: Part 4 – Building a Night Market Plan

passage.text: Art college students wanted a night market where local makers could sell handmade goods after dark. They chose an old car park near the river because it was empty on Friday evenings. The students drew a map showing each stall and the visitor entrance. (16) ..... After checking the measurements again, they submitted the final version to the council for a safety inspection.

The first challenge was lighting, because the car park had only two working lamps. An engineering student designed battery-powered fairy lights hung between wooden poles. The college lent the poles from its theatre department, and a shop donated the necessary cable. (17) ..... A photographer captured the finished scene from the bridge, and the image was shared widely by local residents.

Thirty makers joined the opening night, selling goods from printed scarves to wooden phone stands. The students asked sellers to keep prices below twenty pounds. A food van at the entrance offered hot soup and bread to anyone wanting a break. (18) ..... The food van owner was pleased with the response and asked to return every week for the rest of term.

Rain threatened the second market, so the team had to cancel or find cover. A student contacted a marquee company that lent two large tents in exchange for advertising space. Visitors said the tents made the event feel cosier than the open car park. (19) ..... Impressed by the organisation, the marquee company later offered the students a discount for any future events.

By the end of term, the market attracted two hundred visitors each week. The college featured it in its prospectus, and three students found part-time work managing stalls. The group planned to continue through summer with a smaller team. (20) ..... A lecturer praised the project for combining creativity with careful organisation. More importantly, the students understood how to negotiate with suppliers, respond to bad weather and share responsibility when decisions had to be made quickly.

parts.passageTitle: Part 5 – Evening Food and New Friends

passage.text: The visitors usually meet (21) ........ Saturday. New members are shown how to (22) ........ the equipment. They can ask for advice if they are (23) ........ about a task. The group works together (24) ........ everyone can learn. Members often share ideas (25) ........ the session. The project has become a popular way to meet (26) ........ people. Visitors can try food from several stalls, but the organisers ask everyone to keep the walkways clear. Families often meet friends there after work, and stallholders enjoy explaining how traditional dishes are prepared. The market has also become a chance for small businesses to test new recipes and learn which foods local people prefer. The organisers change a few stalls each month so that regular visitors can try something different. Cooks are asked to describe common ingredients clearly, and volunteers help families find quieter places to sit. The friendly atmosphere is one reason the event attracts both local residents and visitors from nearby towns.

They can join the work, (29) ........ they should follow the group’s instructions. The project has kept useful materials (30) ........ being thrown away. It is a place (31) ........ people can exchange ideas. Remember (32) ........ ask for help when you need it. The event is now held regularly because it brings people together without requiring a large venue. Volunteers collect rubbish during the evening and check that the cooking areas are safe. At the end, the organisers review comments from visitors and use them when planning the next market. The market has become part of the neighbourhood calendar. People come for the food, but they also hear music, meet local producers and learn about community activities. The organisers hope to keep the event affordable while giving small traders a chance to grow.
